subject: physics
question_text: What is the principle of a pressure cooker?

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 11 Very Short Answer Question 16 (printed p.117). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The 1 + 1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: a pressure cooker is sealed so the steam it generates cannot escape, raising the pressure inside above atmospheric; the boiling point of water rises with pressure, so the water inside boils well above 100 °C, and the food cooks faster because it is cooked at that higher temperature, not simply because the steam is trapped.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: How the pressure rises
steps.mark_note: Sealed lid traps steam, pressure rises
lines: A pressure cooker is a closed vessel with
a tightly fitting lid, so the steam formed
This raises the pressure inside well
steps.margin_note: First mark. Say the cooker is sealed so steam cannot escape, and the pressure inside rises above atmospheric.
steps.why: A pressure cooker works because it is sealed: with nowhere for the steam to go, more of it collects inside the same volume, and that is what raises the pressure above atmospheric.
common_mistakes: Saying the steam is trapped and stopping there, without saying what that does to the pressure inside.

recall.must_convey: That a pressure cooker is sealed so the steam cannot escape, and this raises the pressure inside above atmospheric.
accept: closed vessel traps the steam and pressure builds

steps.memory_tip: Sealed lid, no escape for the steam: pressure inside climbs.

steps.label: Why the food cooks faster
lines: The boiling point of water rises as the
pressure on it rises. Inside the cooker
the water boils at a temperature well
Food cooks faster because it is cooked
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Say the boiling point rises with the pressure, so the water boils well above 100 °C and the food is cooked at that higher temperature.
steps.why: A higher pressure alone does not cook food faster — what matters is that the boiling point of water rises with pressure, so the water inside is well above 100 °C, and it is that higher temperature that cooks the food faster.
common_mistakes: Saying the food cooks faster simply because the steam is trapped, without saying the pressure raises the boiling point and the water reaches a higher temperature.

recall.must_convey: That the boiling point of water rises with pressure, so the water inside boils well above 100 °C and the food cooks faster at that higher temperature.
accept: water boils above 100 degrees Celsius inside
food cooks at the higher temperature, not because steam is trapped

steps.memory_tip: Higher pressure, higher boiling point, hotter water — that is what cooks the food faster.

insider_note: Two ideas complete this answer: the sealed cooker raising the pressure, and the higher pressure raising the boiling point so the food is cooked at a higher temperature — not simply that the steam is trapped.
